outcome: No proof of P = NP or of P ≠ NP has been accepted since 26 January 2024. The Clay Institute page still reads 'Unsolved' and a September 2026 tracker lists the problem as open with no completed AI solution. The events found are unrefereed P = NP and P ≠ NP preprints, a 2023 P ≠ NP pilot with GPT-4 that is not a checked proof, a 2025 published comment rejecting a restricted P ≠ NP argument, and neighbouring results (time versus space, arithmetic circuits for the permanent) that do not address P vs NP.
problem_asks: Whether P = NP: whether every decision problem whose yes-instances have certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time can also be decided in deterministic polynomial time. The statement as given names only 'P versus NP problem' and lists no sub-parts. Either answer (P = NP or P ≠ NP) would resolve it. The Clay page describes it informally as 'P (i.e., easy to find) versus NP (i.e., easy to check)'.

events.what_happened: Qingxiu Dong, Li Dong, Ke Xu, Guangyan Zhou, Yaru Hao, Zhifang Sui and Furu Wei post 'Large Language Model for Science: A Study on P vs. NP' (arXiv:2309.05689). In a pilot study, GPT-4 is prompted through five personas and a Socratic dialogue; the abstract says it 'successfully produces a proof schema and engages in rigorous reasoning throughout 97 dialogue turns' and concludes P ≠ NP, which the authors say aligns with Xu and Zhou (2023). The authors present it as a pilot, not a verified proof.
events.revisions: v1 11 Sep 2023 is the only version I saw. Later versions were not checked.
events.delivers: Establishes only that a dialogue with GPT-4, under the authors' own prompt design, produced a P ≠ NP-concluding argument. It is not a checked proof. The authors' own transcript margin notes say that 'the answer provided by GPT-4 here is not rigorous' and that 'LLM responses may contain hallucinations'. Restricted to a pilot study.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. No separation or resolution is established.
events.directly_checkable: The 97-turn dialogue transcript is in section 3.2 of the paper and can be read by hand. I read only the visible part of it, not line by line.
events.doubts: The authors' own margin notes: 'prompting directly on how to prove P!=NP may lead the model to retrieve related work' and 'the answer provided by GPT-4 here is not rigorous'. The authors designed the prompts: five roles, custom system instructions (Appendix A, not read), and turns 3 and 13 ask for a proof-by-contradiction idea. What the model was asked to find is therefore the authors' choice. No refereed check was found.
events.direction: Asserts P ≠ NP. This cuts against P = NP if correct, but the argument is not checked.

systems.name: GPT-4
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors' abstract, it produced a proof schema and carried out the reasoning over 97 dialogue turns, concluding P ≠ NP. The authors steer it through five personas and system instructions they wrote. The authors credit the model with the argument; they do not say a human checked it.
systems.basis_quote: GPT-4 successfully produces a proof schema and engages in rigorous reasoning throughout 97 dialogue turns

events.what_happened: Ke Xu and Guangyan Zhou post 'SAT Requires Exhaustive Search' (arXiv:2302.09512, first version 19 Feb 2023). They construct self-referential CSP and SAT instances (large domains; long clauses) and argue by diagonalisation that they cannot be solved without exhaustive search. The latest arXiv version (v9, 28 Oct 2024) says this is stronger than P ≠ NP. The paper appeared in Frontiers of Computer Science in 2025 (Springer DOI 10.1007/s11704-025-50231-4; the Springer page redirected to a login and was not read, so the journal details come from search snippets).
events.revisions: v1 19 Feb 2023; v2 28 Feb 2023; v3 19 Mar 2023; v4 4 Apr 2023; v5 22 Apr 2023; v6 14 Aug 2023; v7 18 Sep 2023; v8 21 Sep 2023; v9 28 Oct 2024. Per a search snippet, v2 carried the title 'Hard Examples Requiring Exhaustive Search do Exist' and a weaker P ≠ NP conclusion; not opened. Journal version in Frontiers of Computer Science, 2025.
events.delivers: For the constructed CSP and SAT families it defines (large-domain CSPs; SAT with long clauses), it claims exhaustive search is necessary. That is restricted to those families. The latest version says the conclusion is stronger than P ≠ NP. The construction does not by itself address general SAT, and the bridge from the constructed families to general P ≠ NP is what the critiques dispute.
events.remains: P vs NP for all of NP. The claim covers only the constructed families, and the authors' step to general P ≠ NP is disputed.

checked_by.qualification: Complexity theorists (Rutgers and MIT). Williams is also the author of williams-2025-square-root-space.
checked_by.what_they_did: Published a comment in the same journal saying the paper 'falls far short of a proof' because it 'makes an assumption about all possible SAT algorithms that is unwarranted'.

checked_by.who: Michael C. Chavrimootoo, Yumeng He, Matan Kotler-Berkowitz, Harry Liuson, Zeyu Nie
checked_by.qualification: Not established in this run; the arXiv page lists names only.
checked_by.what_they_did: Posted an objection (arXiv:2312.02071, Dec 2023). See chavrimootoo-2023-critique.

events.time_since_posted: 3 years 8 months since first posting; last arXiv revision Oct 2024
events.directly_checkable: The constructed instances are described, but their hardness is argued for all algorithms, not exhibited. Nothing can be checked by hand without the construction, which I did not read in full.
events.doubts: Two outside objections, both on the same point: Chavrimootoo et al. (Dec 2023) argue the required algorithm structure 'is not guaranteed to exist'; Allender and Williams (2025) call the assumption about all SAT algorithms unwarranted. The authors replied in Jan 2024 (xu-zhou-2024-further-explanations) and cite a reply titled 'Self-reference as key to proving extreme hardness' (from a 2025 reference list; not found). The claimed scope changed across versions (title, and whether the conclusion implies P ≠ NP or something stronger).
events.direction: Claims that for the constructed families exhaustive search is needed, and that this implies P ≠ NP (the latest version says stronger). It cuts toward P ≠ NP if correct, but only for those families. Critics say the bridge to general P ≠ NP is unsupported.
events.object: A family of constructed self-referential CSP and SAT instances, built by a diagonalisation-style argument. The claim is that no algorithm avoids exhaustive search on them. The hardness is argued across all algorithms, not exhibited as a short certificate.

events.what_happened: Qingxiu Dong, Guangyan Zhou and Ke Xu post 'Further Explanations on SAT Requires Exhaustive Search' (arXiv:2401.01193, 2 Jan 2024). It responds to 'misinterpretations' of the 2023 paper and to 'feedback received on our prior paper', and clarifies the assumptions of Lemma 3.1. It adds no new theorem about P vs NP.
events.delivers: A clarification of the 2023 argument (algorithm designability, white-box diagonalisation, an 'almost independent solution space'). It establishes no new result.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, and the 2023 claim's scope as above.
events.doubts: This is the authors' own reply. No outside engagement with this clarification was found.
events.direction: Same as xu-zhou-2023-sat-exhaustive: restricted to the constructed families, with the authors' stated implication for P ≠ NP.

events.what_happened: Michael C. Chavrimootoo, Yumeng He, Matan Kotler-Berkowitz, Harry Liuson and Zeyu Nie post 'Evaluating the Claims of SAT Requires Exhaustive Search' (arXiv:2312.02071, 4 Dec 2023). They argue the Xu–Zhou argument assumes an algorithm for Model RB has a structure that leverages downward self-reducibility, and that this structure 'is not guaranteed to exist', so the paper 'neither proves SETH to be true nor proves P ≠ NP'.
events.delivers: No positive result. It establishes a specific objection to the 2023 argument: an unproven structural assumption about algorithms for Model RB.
events.remains: Not applicable: this is a critique.

checked_by.who: Michael C. Chavrimootoo, Yumeng He, Matan Kotler-Berkowitz, Harry Liuson, Zeyu Nie
checked_by.qualification: Not established in this run; the arXiv page lists names only.
checked_by.what_they_did: Worked through the 2023 paper and posted an objection to its main structural assumption.

events.doubts: The objection is an arXiv abstract stage posting, not a refereed comment. A search snippet (not read in full) says it found no fault in Section 2 of the original paper, so its scope is narrower than a full rejection. I read only the abstract.
events.direction: Cuts against the Xu–Zhou claim: argues it does not establish P ≠ NP.

events.what_happened: Eric Allender and Ryan Williams publish 'Comment on SAT requires exhaustive search' in Frontiers of Computer Science (published online 1 Sep 2025; vol. 20, issue 1, 2026; DOI 10.1007/s11704-025-53000-5). The comment says the article 'claims to show that the SAT problem requires at least 2^{δn} time', 'falls far short of a proof', and 'makes an assumption about all possible SAT algorithms that is unwarranted'.
events.delivers: No result of its own. It establishes that the 2^{δn} SAT bound claimed in the 2023 paper is not proved, on the stated ground.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. The comment does not address P vs NP directly.

checked_by.who: Eric Allender (Rutgers University) and Ryan Williams (Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
checked_by.qualification: Complexity theorists, publishing in the same journal as the paper they comment on.
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a published comment identifying an unwarranted assumption in the argument.

events.doubts: The authors' reply, cited in a 2025 reference list as 'Self-reference as key to proving extreme hardness', was not found, so the exchange after the comment is not known.
events.direction: Against the Xu–Zhou claim.

events.what_happened: T. S. Arthanari, 'Pedigree Polytopes' (Springer monograph, 2023 per a search snippet; Springer DOI 10.1007/978-981-19-9952-9 per a redirect; the page redirected to a login and was not read). A publisher blurb quoted in a search snippet says that by showing STSP has a polynomial algorithm, the book 'settles the P vs NP question'. The kind field has no 'book' option, so 'journal' is used here as the closest.
events.delivers: Per the blurb only: a polynomial algorithm for the symmetric TSP via pedigree-polytope membership, which the book says settles P vs NP. The 2025 arXiv preprint says the material 'appears in the book' and is 'not published in a refereed journal'.
events.remains: Per the blurb, nothing. The blurb is not a referee's assessment.
events.doubts: The arXiv 2025 comment says the material is 'not published in a refereed journal' and asks for expert vetting. A search snippet cites an older Springer chapter by Arthanari (LNCS 2013) whose necessary condition for membership is shown not sufficient by a counterexample. That is an earlier condition, not this claim; the snippet was not opened.
events.direction: Claims P = NP through STSP, per the blurb.

events.what_happened: T. S. Arthanari posts 'On the Importance of Studying the Membership Problem for Pedigree Polytopes' (arXiv:2507.09069, 11 Jul 2025). The abstract (as read) says membership for pedigree polytopes can be decided in strongly polynomial time, with consequences for linear optimisation over these polytopes and for the symmetric TSP, and that it 'claims the result implies NP = P'. The comments field says the article 'contains material not published in a refereed journal, but appears in the book by Springer' and is 'mainly for expert vetting of its proofs and concepts'.
events.delivers: Claims a strongly polynomial membership test for pedigree polytopes and, through the symmetric TSP, P = NP. The author says the purpose is expert vetting.
events.remains: Whether the membership result holds. The P = NP step is the claimed route.
events.doubts: The author labels the material as not refereed and asks for expert vetting. The same material appears in an earlier monograph (arthanari-2023-springer-book).
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: T. S. Arthanari posts 'Lean 4 Machine-Verified Proof of P = NP via the Pedigree Polytope Membership Problem' (arXiv:2606.03194, 2 Jun 2026; one version; 33 pages). The abstract says the membership problem is solvable in strongly polynomial time, which implies the symmetric TSP is polynomial and 'resolves P vs. NP'. The main result is named p_equals_np. A Lean 4/Mathlib4 project of 36 files is linked at github.com/TiruArt/Pedigree-Polytopes-Lean4. The GitHub page was not opened.
events.delivers: Claims a Lean-verified theorem p_equals_np that P = NP via the symmetric-TSP reduction. The Lean check establishes the stated formal theorem. Whether its definitions of P and NP and its reduction are faithful to the standard ones is not established in any source.
events.remains: Nothing, if the formal statement is faithful. Faithfulness is the open question.
events.directly_checkable: The Lean repository, which I did not open. Checking it would mean reading the formal statement of p_equals_np and the definitions it uses against the standard ones.
events.doubts: A Lean check verifies the formal statement, not that it captures P and NP. The mathematical route is the same as the 2025 preprint. A search snippet (not opened) cites a 2013 Springer chapter that shows an earlier Arthanari necessary condition is not sufficient, so the membership question was contested before this claim. No outside expert engagement was found.
events.direction: Claims P = NP, in Lean.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega posts 'Note for the P versus NP Problem' on Cambridge Open Engage as a working paper (posted 30 Jan 2024, nine versions to 22 Apr 2024). It states: 'We show that the Monotone Weighted 2-satisfiability problem (MW2SAT) is NP-complete and P at the same time', and so P = NP. The page says it 'has not been peer-reviewed by Cambridge University Press at the time of posting'. The page says a version was later published in IPI Letters on 7 Jun 2024 (DOI 10.59973/ipil.92).
events.revisions: Nine Cambridge versions to 22 Apr 2024 (per the page). IPI Letters 7 Jun 2024. Search snippets (not opened) describe later EasyChair versions renaming the problem MWX2SAT, switching to K-CLOSURE on directed graphs, and changing one K-CLOSURE definition from OR to AND in version 10.
events.delivers: Claims a polynomial-time algorithm for MW2SAT, an NP-complete problem, which would give P = NP. The claim is about one NP-complete problem. If it held, it would settle the problem. The page gives no proof detail.
events.remains: Everything, unless the claim is verified.
events.directly_checkable: The MW2SAT algorithm is in the paper, which I did not read in full. A hand test on small instances would be the check.
events.doubts: A single assertion, with no outside engagement found. The version history in snippets shows the argument changed between versions (a flawed route removed in version 8; a definition changed in version 10). The journal named (IPI Letters) shares its name with the author's institute, Information Physics Institute. I did not check the publisher relationship or whether it refereed the paper.
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: Vega's preprints.org manuscript 202409.2053. A search snippet gives the first version as 26 Sep 2024 and a latest version (v21) dated 22 Jul 2026, titled 'P vs NP', claiming a polynomial algorithm for SAT that 'establishes that P equals NP'. The page returned HTTP 403 when fetched, so this rests on the search snippet. The page is marked not peer-reviewed.
events.revisions: Per snippet: about 21 versions to v21 (22 Jul 2026). Titles run 'Note for the P versus NP problem (II)', then 'SAT in Polynomial Time: A Proof of P = NP', then 'P vs NP'.
events.delivers: Claims a polynomial-time algorithm for SAT, which would give P = NP. The snippet gives no algorithm detail.
events.remains: Everything, unless the claim is verified.
events.doubts: Not read (403). Per snippets, the framing hardened from 'potentially establishing' the equivalence (2024) to 'establishes' it (v21). The same author's EngrXiv series (vega-2024-12-engrxiv) shows 16 versions in about ten weeks.
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: Vega's EngrXiv preprint 'SAT in Polynomial Time: A Proof of P = NP' (engrxiv 4189; posted 4 Dec 2024; versions to 19 Feb 2025 listed, version 16 the latest). It claims SAT, 'traditionally considered NP-complete, can be solved in polynomial time, establishing the equivalence of P and NP'. The page lists no revision note for version 2.
events.revisions: Sixteen versions, from 4 Dec 2024 (v1) through 19 Feb 2025 (v16), per the page's version list. Version dates include 10 Dec 2024, 11 Dec, 13 Dec, 16 Dec, 17 Dec, 20 Dec, 21 Dec, 23 Dec, 28 Dec 2024, and 15 Jan, 16 Jan, 20 Jan, 22 Jan, 27 Jan, 19 Feb 2025.
events.delivers: Claims polynomial-time SAT, which would give P = NP. The scope is SAT alone; the equivalence follows from SAT being NP-complete.
events.remains: Everything, unless the SAT algorithm is verified.
events.directly_checkable: The Python sample implementation is not referenced on this page. The SAT algorithm would need to be run on hard instances.
events.doubts: Sixteen versions in about ten weeks: the argument was revised repeatedly. A search snippet (not verified on the page I read) describes a version-2 note admitting a reduction gap ('the induced graph was not necessarily bipartite'). The page I fetched shows no such note, so the two sources disagree and I did not resolve it. The snippet also reports that the introduction concedes most researchers believe P ≠ NP.
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: Changryeol Lee posts 'Graph-Based Deterministic Polynomial Framwork for NP Problems' (arXiv:2508.13166, 2 Aug 2025; later titled 'Graph-Based Deterministic Polynomial Algorithm for NP Problems'). The abstract claims 'a constructive proof that P=NP' via a graph of computation edges for a deterministic verifier over all certificates, 'applicable to all NP problems without requiring reduction to an NP-complete problem', and says the construction 'provides a direct resolution to the P versus NP question'. arXiv lists the author as 'Independent Researcher'. Search snippets give a Yonsei affiliation and the PDF metadata a KAIST email; these were not resolved.
events.delivers: Claims that every NP problem is decidable in deterministic polynomial time, i.e. P = NP, with no restriction in the abstract as read. The mechanism is edge extension over all certificate paths, with a 'local infeasibility trimming tool'. If correct, it resolves the whole problem.
events.remains: Nothing separately, if correct. The full claim rests on the mechanism.
events.doubts: (1) The comment on version 8 (Jul 2026) says it adds 'a certificate-oblivious verifier Turing machine and grid-aligned footmarks' to 'strengthen the total collapse property'. The mechanism was still being changed fourteen months after posting. (2) Per a search snippet (not on the abstract page I read), the follow-up arXiv:2602.10991 says some components are 'intentionally left abstract' and that no explicit finite-state machines are given for the NP verifiers. (3) The PDF body was unreadable in this run, so the argument itself was not read.
events.direction: Claims P = NP for all NP problems.

events.what_happened: Lee posts 'Implementation of Polynomial NP-Complete Algorithms Based on the NP Verifier Simulation Framework' (arXiv:2602.10991; submitted 11 Feb 2026; v4 12 Jul 2026). Per the abstract as read, it builds deterministic certificate-oblivious verifier Turing machines for SAT and Subset-Sum, improves the feasible-graph construction, and provides a Python implementation with a public repository (the repository was not opened).
events.delivers: Explicit verifier machines and an implementation for SAT and Subset-Sum, presented as an extension of the 2508.13166 framework. The abstract as read does not itself state P = NP.
events.remains: P vs NP for NP as a whole. Per the abstract, explicit machines are given for two problems only.
events.directly_checkable: The Python implementation in the public repository (not opened).
events.doubts: Per the search snippet, the earlier framework is established 'at a formal level' with components left abstract; that sentence is not on the abstract page I read.
events.direction: Consistent with the P = NP framework of lee-2025-graph-based, for two problems. Does not itself claim P = NP as read.

events.what_happened: Mirzakhmet Syzdykov (independent researcher) posts 'NP-complete Problems can be Solved and Verified in Polynomial Time' (EngrXiv 5533; posted 8 Oct 2025, updated 14 Oct 2025). The abstract says: 'In this short paper we give the final resolution of "P versus NP" theorem according to our previous results obtained in the field of automaton implementation for extended regular expressions and generally intersection operator.' The keywords include 'P versus NP' and 'Verification'.
events.delivers: Claims a final resolution with P = NP as the keyword implies. The abstract as read gives no proof detail. A search snippet (not on the page) says the argument checks solutions and builds a decision tree in polynomial time.
events.remains: Everything, as no mechanism is shown on the page read.
events.doubts: The same author's later EngrXiv 6770 (2026; snippet only) claims the opposite, a proof of nonequivalence between polynomial and non-polynomial classes, and an earlier paper concludes P = EXPTIME = NP (snippet only). The author's position is inconsistent across the series. The server does not peer-review.
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: Syzdykov's EngrXiv 6770, 'Linear Algorithm for Regular Expressions within P vs. NP Question' (copyright 2026 per a search snippet). Per the snippet, it claims an almost-polynomial matching algorithm for regular expressions with intersection, complement and subtraction, and a proof of nonequivalence between polynomial and non-polynomial classes. The page was not opened.
events.revisions: Earlier version 'Almost Polynomial Matching with Extended Regular Expressions' (EngrXiv 5908) has the same abstract, per snippet.
events.delivers: Per snippet only: a claimed nonequivalence of polynomial and non-polynomial classes, which would contradict the P = NP claim in syzdykov-2025-engrxiv-5533.
events.remains: Unknown; not read.
events.doubts: Not read. Included because it contradicts the same author's 2025 claim.
events.direction: Per snippet: against P = NP (nonequivalence).

events.what_happened: Sanal Ednyashev's Zenodo preprint 'Formal Proof that P = NP via Logical Tabular Machine (LTM)' (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.15377460). The version read is v2, dated 10 May 2025; the record notes that a newer version exists. The abstract says it contains 'a formal, constructive proof that the complexity classes P and NP are equal', using a deterministic Logical Tabular Machine that propagates local truth-table constraints. It claims polynomial running time O(m²·n) and coverage of 21 classic NP-complete problems. Files: PDF, LaTeX source, a Python sample implementation, and test cases.
events.revisions: v2 10 May 2025 (as read); the first version's date was not established; a newer version is noted on the page.
events.delivers: Claims a polynomial-time method for 21 named NP-complete problems. The record does not show coverage of every problem in NP, which a P = NP conclusion would need.
events.remains: Coverage of all of NP, which the record's 21 named problems do not show.
events.directly_checkable: The Python sample implementation in the record's files. The files were not accessible for checking in this run.
events.doubts: 'Formal Proof' is in the title, but no proof-assistant artifact is listed in the metadata. Listing 21 NP-complete problems is not coverage of NP. Files restricted, so the code was not run.
events.direction: Claims P = NP.

events.what_happened: Joe Gallagher posts 'Hamiltonian Route: Separator Interface States and the Anti-Stitch Framework' (Zenodo 19103649, 18 Mar 2026). The record claims that every Boolean fan-in-2 circuit computing the Hamiltonian Cycle function HAM_n on n vertices has size 2^Ω(n), improving on prior polynomial lower bounds for explicit NP functions, and says it 'is supplemented by' github.com/Mintpath/p-neq-np-lean. The Lean package p_ne_np (owner Mintpath, on Reservoir) says it gives 'Machine-verified proof (0 sorries, 2 axioms) that P ≠ NP via exponential circuit lower bounds for Hamiltonian Cycle'. The axioms are not listed on that page. The GitHub repository returned HTTP 404 when fetched.
events.revisions: Zenodo v1 18 Mar 2026. The Reservoir package page shows 'last updated' 25 Jul 2026 and Lean 4.28.0 as the build toolchain (other toolchains fail, per the page).
events.delivers: Claims an unconditional 2^Ω(n) lower bound for fan-in-2 circuits computing HAM_n. The package claims this yields P ≠ NP through its own step. The scope is one explicit NP function and one circuit model. The record calls the previous bounds polynomial, so the claimed step is very large.
events.remains: P vs NP is resolved only if the bound holds and the package's step to P ≠ NP is sound. Neither has been checked in any source.
events.directly_checkable: The HAM_n circuit lower bound is a claim about all fan-in-2 circuits. The Lean package is the only artefact to check, and I did not examine it, because the GitHub repository returned 404.
events.doubts: (1) The claimed bound is far beyond the prior bounds the record itself describes. No outside engagement was found. (2) The package has 2 axioms, not listed on its page. A search snippet names one, 'lambda_le_sum_leafWidth_of_circuit', not verified. (3) The GitHub repository returned 404 when fetched. (4) 'sorry_free: true' is self-reported on the package page. (5) The link between the author name on Zenodo (Gallagher) and the owner name on the repository (Mintpath) is the Zenodo record's own; I did not verify it.
events.direction: Claims P ≠ NP, via an exponential circuit lower bound for one NP function.
events.object: A claimed proof that every fan-in-2 Boolean circuit computing the Hamiltonian Cycle function HAM_n on n vertices has size 2^Ω(n). Non-constructive as an argument over all circuits; no specific circuit is exhibited.

events.what_happened: A self-published Google Doc by 'Donald Lippy', titled as a Clay Millennium Problem paper and dated 5 June 2025 (per a search snippet), claims P ≠ NP by combining diagonalisation, hierarchy theorems and a sequence of lemmas, and says that assuming P = NP contradicts established class separations. The document returned HTTP 400 and HTTP redirects when fetched, so this rests on the search excerpt.
events.delivers: Claims P ≠ NP. Per the search excerpt only.
events.remains: Everything, unless the argument is checked.
events.doubts: Per the search excerpt (not verified in the full text), the paper defines NP as the class verifiable in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine, which is not the standard definition. The proof section was cut off in the excerpt, so the contradiction step could not be checked.
events.direction: Claims P ≠ NP.

events.what_happened: R. Ryan Williams posts 'Simulating Time With Square-Root Space' (arXiv:2502.17779, 25 Feb 2025). It shows any multitape Turing machine running in time t(n) ≥ n can be simulated in O(√(t log t)) space, improving on Hopcroft, Paul and Valiant (1975). The abstract says the work makes 'a little progress on the P versus PSPACE problem'. A search snippet says it was accepted to STOC 2025 (not verified on the page).
events.delivers: Establishes a time-to-space simulation bound and a separation for explicit problems solvable in O(n) space but not in n^{2−ε} time on a multitape Turing machine (per the abstract as read). This concerns time and space, and P vs PSPACE, not P vs NP.
events.remains: P vs NP itself: untouched. The abstract calls its progress on P vs PSPACE 'a little'.
events.doubts: Engagement with the result exists (search snippets cite Fortnow's blog and Quanta coverage; not opened), but none that I found addresses P vs NP.
events.direction: Neighbouring result. No direction on P vs NP.

events.what_happened: Wen Fang, Xianxian Li, Jun Liu, Jie Luo, Yongxin Tong and Ke Xu post 'Self-Referential K-SAT and the Finite Analogue of Gödel's Incompleteness Theorem' (arXiv:2607.01671, 2 Jul 2026; v2 20 Sep 2026). It shows that local subinstances of a random CNF ensemble look identical to a bounded query evaluator, and derives resolution, algebraic and proof-size lower bounds. The authors state the construction is 'not itself a time-complexity lower bound'.
events.revisions: v1 2 Jul 2026; v2 20 Sep 2026 ('some results revised and new results added').
events.delivers: A finite propositional self-reference construction for K-SAT. The authors disclaim a time-complexity lower bound and do not claim P vs NP.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: No direction on P vs NP; the authors disclaim a time-complexity lower bound.

events.what_happened: OpenAI publishes 'Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science' (1 Aug 2026, per secondary coverage). The OpenAI page returned HTTP 403 and was not read. Per secondary coverage, the ten results came from an unreleased internal version of 'Astra', each with a Lean 4 certificate in a GitHub repository (openai/ten-proofs, per coverage). One result gives new lower bounds for arithmetic circuits and formulas computing the permanent, including an arithmetic-formula bound of order n⁴/log n.
events.delivers: Per secondary coverage only: lower bounds for the permanent in arithmetic circuit and formula models. This is an algebraic question (VP vs VNP type), not P vs NP. The formula bound is polynomial, not superpolynomial.
events.remains: P vs NP is not addressed. The arithmetic analogue is also open at the superpolynomial level, per coverage.
events.directly_checkable: The Lean certificates (openai/ten-proofs, per coverage; not opened). Lean certifies the formal statement, not whether it matches the intended claim.
events.doubts: Entirely from secondary coverage, since the primary page was unreachable. One snippet attributes a claim to Levent Alpöge that a public model reproduced five of the ten results; uncorroborated, and not about P vs NP.
events.direction: Neighbouring algebraic result. No direction on P vs NP.

ai.disclosed_cost: One secondary report gives roughly $2,000 at API rates. Not from OpenAI's page; unverified.

events.what_happened: Vinay Deolalikar, of HP Labs, circulates a 103-page manuscript claiming P ≠ NP in early August 2010. Scott Aaronson's blog post 'Eight Signs A Claimed P≠NP Proof Is Wrong' (13 Aug 2010) lists failures: the argument does not explain why the proof fails for 2SAT and XOR-SAT; it ignores known polynomial-time techniques; it proves no weaker results along the way. It says 'a clear consensus has emerged that the proof, as it stands, is fatally flawed' and that 'Vinay Deolalikar still hasn't retracted his P≠NP claim'. The search did not establish a formal arXiv posting.

disputes.summary: Xu and Zhou's 2023 claim that constructed SAT and CSP families require exhaustive search, and that this implies P ≠ NP, is disputed by Chavrimootoo et al. (Dec 2023) and by Allender and Williams (2025), who call an assumption about all SAT algorithms unwarranted. The authors defended the paper in Jan 2024. The record does not pick a winner.

Incompatible claims in the record: P = NP (Vega 2024–2025, Syzdykov 2025, Arthanari 2025 and 2026, Lee 2025, Ednyashev 2025, Arthanari's 2023 monograph) against P ≠ NP (Dong 2023 with GPT-4, Xu and Zhou 2023 for constructed families, Gallagher 2026, Lippy 2025, Deolalikar 2010). Syzdykov's own 2026 snippet claims nonequivalence, contradicting his 2025 P = NP claim. These cannot all be right.

summary: Searches found no accepted resolution of P vs NP, and no event that a named expert has publicly verified. Two sources I opened state the status: the Clay page (claymath.org/millennium-problems/p-vs-np/) reads 'Unsolved', and the Kingy tracker (last verified 11 Sep 2026) lists the problem 'Open' with no completed AI solution. Wikipedia's article, as fetched in this run (the current revision, not the frozen January 2024 one), says the problem 'is generally considered unsolved' and records 116 purported proofs from 1986 to 2016 (Woeginger's list), which I did not record one by one. Since 26 Jan 2024 I found 16 events, all unrefereed preprints or a 2025 comment, plus several neighbouring results. The strongest-looking event is Arthanari's June 2026 Lean preprint, but the Lean check covers only the formal statement, and the faithfulness of its P and NP definitions is unexamined. Gallagher's March 2026 exponential circuit bound for Hamiltonian Cycle claims P ≠ NP with a Lean package, but its GitHub repository returned 404, and its claimed step is very large relative to the prior bounds the record itself reports. The Xu and Zhou line is the most-engaged event: two outside objections (2023, 2025) and an author defence (2024), with no resolution in the record. Several close calls: (a) Xu and Zhou's constructed families are a restricted claim that the authors say implies more than P ≠ NP, and the critics dispute only the bridge, so one reading counts it as a partial result on a scoped question while the other reads it as no progress on P vs NP; (b) the Vega series is in-window (first posted 30 Jan 2024, four days after the frozen revision), and its status depends on whether the IPI Letters publication was refereed, which I did not establish. AI involvement: the only AI-system claim about a P vs NP argument that I could source from the authors is Dong et al.'s 2023 GPT-4 pilot, which the authors credit with producing the proof schema and concluding P ≠ NP, but which they also describe as not rigorous. Every other AI claim I found concerns different problems: OpenAI's Aug 2026 permanent bound (arithmetic analogue; primary page unreachable, so no authors' quote could be taken), and OpenAI's Sept 2026 Navier–Stokes claim. A ChatSlide article headlined 'Next Target: P vs NP' (10 Sep 2026) traces the P vs NP idea to one X post by an individual researcher (Yam Peleg), not to OpenAI, and says OpenAI and DrLambda are collaborating on an unnamed 'final result'. A second report of an OpenAI run on 'six remaining problems' including P vs NP (1 Sep 2026) was not verified. I did not find any lab announcement naming P vs NP. Fortnow's June 2026 post says he cannot get an AI to produce a full Lean-verified proof of P closed under complement and does not expect a P vs NP proof 'proven by man or machine' in his lifetime; it reports no AI result on P vs NP. The 'proof skeletons' claim in a FutureSearch forecast page (Aug 2026) could not be traced to a source; the cited CACM link is a different article per a search summary. Pre-window history is recorded in full for the events I found; the 1986–2016 catalogue (Woeginger) is only summarised.
competing_reading: The strongest case for reading the record differently: (1) Arthanari's June 2026 preprint (arthanari-2026-lean-arxiv) is the only event with a machine-checked artefact, and if the formal theorem is faithful it would settle the problem as stated, so the outstanding question reduces to one reading of p_equals_np. (2) Xu and Zhou's constructions can be read as a genuine restricted separation: the claim covers explicit families, and the critics dispute only the bridge to general P ≠ NP. On that reading the event is a partial result on a scoped question, not a null. (3) Dong et al. 2023 can be read as an AI event with load-bearing content, since the authors credit GPT-4 with the proof schema and the P ≠ NP conclusion, even though the authors also call its answers non-rigorous. Against all three: no event has been checked by a named expert in public, and every P = NP claim in the record sits in an unrefereed preprint, so the problem's status is unchanged.
what_would_settle_it: For the Lean claims (arthanari-2026-lean-arxiv; gallagher-2026-zenodo-hamiltonian-route): the axioms listed, the sorry status read from the repository (GitHub pages I could not open), and a reading of the formal definitions of P and NP and of the reductions against the standard ones. For the Xu and Zhou line: the authors' 2025 reply and any referee report for the Frontiers version. For any claimed proof: a refereed publication plus a named expert's written verification or refutation. For the Lippy document and the Vega preprints.org v21: their text, which I could not read. For the OpenAI permanent result: the OpenAI page and Lean repository, to confirm the bound and the AI's role.
